title: Thinking Loop v1: safety scan

D0.outcome: Says in own words the two questions asked before every move (what did their last move threaten; is any of my pieces attacked without enough defence) and why the order matters.

D1.outcome: With prompts on, answers both questions before choosing a move in ten consecutive positions, naming the threat or saying there is none.

D2.outcome: With prompts off, in mixed positions (some with a threat, some without), plays a move that neither ignores a real threat nor wastes a move on a non-threat in at least 8 of 10.

D3.outcome: Keeps the scan when an attacking move is tempting (items built so the attack fails to a one-move reply) and when the position feels safe.

D4.outcome: In own games with prompts off, loses no piece to a one-move threat across ten consecutive games, as shown by the unprompted-behaviour ledger.

misconceptions: The scan is only needed when the position looks dangerous.
Checking my own pieces is enough; the opponent's last move can be ignored.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S2; docs/council-synthesis.md CD-3 (one versioned Thinking Loop)
docs/first-hours.md session 4 (threat check as loop v1)
sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-51 (G1: threat never seen), CI-24 (danger of a safe position)
conditions: Applies at every move; cost is a few seconds; pays most when the last move created a threat or left a piece loose.
The scan answers what is attacked now; it does not replace calculation of forcing lines.
condition_sources: CNC CD-3: v1 is the first version of the loop
contrasts: Running the scan only when 'it feels dangerous'; the champion's oversight in a quiet position shows the habit must be unconditional.
Scanning one's own pieces but not the square the opponent's last move now attacks.
Positions where nothing is attacked on either side; the routine should end quickly with 'no threat'.
